whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Heroku Architect exam for?

personas.label: Hands-on practitioners
personas.description: You build and run apps on Heroku and want to show you can design them for scale, security and uptime.

personas.label: Solution designers
personas.description: You plan solutions where Heroku apps work alongside Salesforce, using Heroku Connect, events or APIs.

personas.label: Career builders
personas.description: You are a developer moving into an architect role on projects that mix Salesforce and custom apps.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Heroku Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: It is a hard exam for people who only know Salesforce, because a lot of it is about running apps: dynos, databases, networking and deployment. You also need to know how Heroku connects to Salesforce.
bullets: 60 scored multiple-choice questions, plus a few unscored ones.
About 63% to pass, about 38 correct answers out of 60. Confirm it in the official exam guide before you book, since Salesforce updates these.
Design choices. Common Runtime or Private Spaces, which data service to use, and how to scale.
Salesforce links. Heroku Connect, events and APIs between Heroku and Salesforce show up often.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: People who have run production apps on Heroku do best. Before you book, aim for 75% or more on practice tests and be able to explain how you would make a Heroku app survive a dyno or database failure.

examFormat.heading: Heroku Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions describe an app with certain needs, such as strict compliance, heavy traffic or a link to Salesforce, and ask which Heroku design fits best.
bestWayToPass: Know the runtimes: Common Runtime, Private Spaces and Shield Private Spaces, and which one each compliance need calls for.
Learn the data services: Heroku Postgres (followers, forks, high availability), Key-Value Store and Apache Kafka on Heroku.
Understand Heroku Connect: How it syncs Salesforce data into Postgres and back, and its limits.
Think twelve-factor: Stateless dynos, config in config vars, and logs as event streams.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests how you design apps on Heroku that scale, stay secure and work with Salesforce. You choose runtimes, data services, deployment flows and integration options.

keyConcepts.h2: Heroku Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Heroku Platform Architecture & Dynos
blocks.body: Heroku apps run in **dynos**, which are lightweight containers. **Web** dynos take HTTP traffic, **worker** dynos run background jobs, and **one-off** dynos run admin tasks. Dynos are stateless: the file system is wiped on restart, and dynos are restarted at least once a day. So any data you need to keep must go to a database, cache or file store such as S3. The router drops requests that take more than 30 seconds, so long work belongs on a worker with a queue. Scale **horizontally** by adding dynos, and **vertically** by choosing larger dyno types. Performance dynos support autoscaling based on response time.

blocks.heading: Data Services: Heroku Postgres & Redis
blocks.body: **Heroku Postgres** is the main managed database. **Followers** are read-only copies that take reporting load off the main database. **Forks** are full copies used for testing or migrations. Higher plans offer **high availability**, with a standby that takes over if the primary fails. **Heroku Key-Value Store** (Redis-compatible) is used for caching, sessions and fast queues. **Apache Kafka on Heroku** handles high-volume event streams between services. Use connection pooling when many dynos connect to one database, so you don't run out of connections.

blocks.heading: CI/CD, Review Apps & Release Management
blocks.body: **Pipelines** move the same build through stages, such as development, staging and production, by promoting it instead of rebuilding. **Review apps** create a temporary app for each pull request, so changes can be tested before merging. **Heroku CI** runs tests on every push. Builds use **buildpacks** or Docker images to turn code into a slug that dynos run. Settings live in **config vars**, not code, so the same build can run in every stage. **Release phase** commands, like database migrations, run before new dynos take traffic. Rollbacks are one command to an earlier release.

blocks.heading: Security, Compliance & Private Spaces
blocks.body: The **Common Runtime** is shared and fine for many apps. **Private Spaces** give you an isolated network in a chosen region, with fixed outbound IPs, internal routing and options to connect to your own network by VPN or peering. **Shield Private Spaces** add stricter controls, such as extra logging and encryption, for regulated data like health records or payment data. Use **Heroku Enterprise** teams with SSO and fine-grained permissions to control who can deploy and change settings. Keep secrets in config vars and limit who can read them.

blocks.heading: Architecture Patterns for Salesforce + Heroku
blocks.body: **Heroku Connect** syncs Salesforce objects with tables in Heroku Postgres, one way or both ways. It suits apps that need to read lots of Salesforce data quickly or write it back without using up API calls in the app. For events, Heroku apps can subscribe to **Platform Events** or **Change Data Capture**, or publish back to Salesforce. For direct calls, apps can use the Salesforce REST API, and Salesforce can call Heroku with **Heroku AppLink** or External Services. A common pattern: customer-facing apps on Heroku handle heavy public traffic, while Salesforce stays the system of record for staff.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Heroku Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions give you an app with one or two firm needs, like compliance, scale or a link to Salesforce. Use those to rule out the designs that almost work.

blocks.heading: Heroku Infrastructure Components
blocks.body: Web dynos for requests, worker dynos for background jobs, one-off dynos for admin tasks. Long work goes to workers with a queue.

blocks.heading: Heroku Connect Architecture
blocks.body: Use Heroku Connect when an app needs fast access to lots of Salesforce data in Postgres. Know that sync isn't instant and that two-way sync needs care with conflicts.

blocks.heading: High Availability & Scaling
blocks.body: Several dynos for the app, a high-availability Postgres plan for the database, and followers for read-heavy reporting.

blocks.heading: Security Architecture
blocks.body: Common Runtime for most apps, Private Spaces for network isolation and fixed IPs, Shield Private Spaces for regulated data.

blocks.heading: Performance Optimization
blocks.body: Cache with Key-Value Store, pool database connections, move slow work off web dynos, and use autoscaling on performance dynos.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Architect Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: After Heroku Architect, many people move toward the wider Salesforce architect credentials:

sampleQuestions.question: A web request sometimes takes 45 seconds because it generates a large PDF. Users see timeout errors. What is the best fix?
options: Move PDF creation to a worker dyno with a queue and tell the user when it is ready
Ask users to refresh the page
sampleQuestions.explanation: The router drops requests over 30 seconds. Background work on a worker dyno avoids the limit and keeps web dynos free.
whyWrong: Refreshing just starts the same slow request again.
A larger dyno may be faster but can still pass 30 seconds.
You can't turn off the router timeout.

sampleQuestions.question: An app saves uploaded images to the dyno's local disk. Images vanish after a while. Why?
options: Dyno file systems are temporary and are wiped when the dyno restarts
sampleQuestions.explanation: Dynos are restarted at least daily and their disk is wiped. Files must go to a store like S3.
whyWrong: Size isn't the cause. Any file on local disk is lost.
The images weren't in the database.
Heroku doesn't target images. The whole local disk is temporary.

sampleQuestions.question: A healthcare app on Heroku will store patient data and must meet strict compliance rules. Which runtime fits?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Shield Private Spaces add the extra isolation, logging and encryption controls needed for regulated data such as health records.
whyWrong: Free or hobby dynos are not suitable for production or compliance.
One-off dynos are for admin tasks, not a runtime choice.
The Common Runtime is shared and not built for regulated data.

sampleQuestions.question: Reporting queries are slowing down the main Heroku Postgres database used by the live app. What should be added?
options: A second app with its own empty database
A follower database for the reports
sampleQuestions.explanation: A follower is a read-only copy that stays in sync. Reports can run on it without slowing the main database.
whyWrong: An empty database has none of the data.
A fork is a one-time copy that quickly goes out of date.
More web dynos don't reduce database load.

sampleQuestions.question: A partner's firewall only allows traffic from fixed IP addresses. Your Heroku app must call the partner's API. What fits?
options: Common Runtime with a random IP
Private Spaces with stable outbound IPs
Calling the partner from the user's browser
sampleQuestions.explanation: Private Spaces give the app fixed outbound IPs that the partner can allow.
whyWrong: Common Runtime IPs change, so the partner can't allow them.
Browser calls come from users' IPs, which are unknown.
Dyno size doesn't change the IP address.

sampleQuestions.question: A customer portal on Heroku needs to read millions of Salesforce Account and Order records quickly, without using up Salesforce API calls on every page view. What should be used?
options: Heroku Connect syncing the records into Heroku Postgres
A REST API call to Salesforce for each page view
Storing the data in config vars
Exporting a CSV from Salesforce each week
sampleQuestions.explanation: Heroku Connect keeps a copy of Salesforce data in Postgres, so the app reads it locally with fast SQL queries.
whyWrong: An API call per page view uses up limits and is slower.
Config vars are for settings, not data.
A weekly CSV is out of date.

sampleQuestions.question: The team wants a temporary test app created for every pull request. Which feature fits?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Review apps spin up a fresh app for each pull request and remove it when the pull request is closed.
whyWrong: Release phase runs tasks before a release, like migrations.
Promotion moves an existing build between stages. It doesn't create per-PR apps.
One-off dynos run single commands.

sampleQuestions.question: A tested build in staging should go to production without being rebuilt. What should the team use?
options: Push the code to production again
Promote the build through a Pipeline
sampleQuestions.explanation: Promotion copies the exact slug from staging to production, so what you tested is what goes live.
whyWrong: Pushing again rebuilds the code, which might not match what was tested.
Copying by hand is error-prone.
A different buildpack produces a different build.

sampleQuestions.question: Database migrations must run before new code starts taking traffic. Where should they run?
options: In a web dyno on first request
sampleQuestions.explanation: Release phase commands run after the build and before new dynos start, so the database is ready first.
whyWrong: Manual steps get missed.
Running on the first request can cause errors for users.
Browsers can't run database migrations.

sampleQuestions.question: A Heroku app should react within seconds when an Opportunity is closed in Salesforce. What fits?
options: Subscribing to Change Data Capture or a Platform Event
Asking sales reps to email the app team
sampleQuestions.explanation: Events push the change to the app as it happens, without polling.
whyWrong: Weekly exports are far too slow.
Hourly polling is slow and wastes API calls.
Email isn't an integration.

sampleQuestions.question: The app stores its database password in the source code. What should be done?
options: Put the password in a comment
Move the password into a config var
sampleQuestions.explanation: Config vars keep settings and secrets out of code, and each environment can have its own values.
whyWrong: A comment is still in the code.
The secret is still in the repository, just harder to read.
A README is even more visible.

sampleQuestions.question: Many dynos connect to one Heroku Postgres database, and the database runs out of connections at peak. What helps most?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Connection pooling shares a smaller number of database connections between many app processes.
whyWrong: More dynos would open even more connections.
Removing indexes slows queries and doesn't reduce connections.
Restarts cause downtime and don't fix the cause.

sampleQuestions.question: The live app's database must keep running if the primary database server fails. What should be chosen?
options: A Heroku Postgres plan with high availability
A follower used for reports only
sampleQuestions.explanation: High-availability plans keep a standby that takes over automatically if the primary fails.
whyWrong: Backups let you restore, but with downtime and some data loss.
A follower can be promoted by hand, but it isn't an automatic failover plan.
Dyno size doesn't protect the database.

sampleQuestions.question: A Heroku app needs a fast cache for user sessions and frequently read data. What should be used?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Key-Value Store (Redis-compatible) is built for fast caching and session storage.
whyWrong: A follower is a read copy of the database, not a cache.
Config vars are for settings.
Local disk is wiped on restart and isn't shared between dynos.

sampleQuestions.question: Many services must exchange a very high volume of events reliably, and new consumers will be added over time. What fits?
options: Sending HTTP calls between every pair of services
sampleQuestions.explanation: Kafka is built for high-volume event streams, and new consumers can read the same stream without changing producers.
whyWrong: Logs aren't a reliable way to deliver events to other services.
Polling a table doesn't scale to high volume.
Point-to-point calls tie services together and grow messy.
